question.text: This Republican won the Presidency in 1880 over Winfield Scott Hancock. Charles Guiteau shot him and he died in July 1881.
question.clue: This man defeated Winfield Scott Hancock to become president, and the Pendleton Civil Service Act was passed after his death.

swap.leadin: He was killed near the end of a June 1876 battle in the Montana territory.
swap.text: Name that 7th Cavalry commander famous for his "last stand."
swap.clue: The Battle of the Rosebud prevented George Crook from joining up with this man, who was killed by the forces of Sitting Bull.

question.text: This Scottish-American philanthropist, a founder of U.S. Steel, unsuccessfully offered to donate $20 million to purchase Filipino independence and counter American imperialism.
question.clue: He wrote that "the man who dies rich, dies disgraced" and he funded many libraries in accordance with his belief that rich men should donate their surpluses back to society.

swap.text: This suffragette worked closely with Elizabeth Cady Stanton in fighting for the right to vote. She was the first woman to be portrayed on an American coin.
swap.clue: This woman is the alleged author of "Marriage and Maternity," an article published in The Revolution.

question.leadin: Answer these questions about the Republican Party.
question.text: Opposing the Half-Breeds, this Republican faction during the late 1800s favored machine type politics. Notable members of this group were Roscoe Conkling and Thomas Platt.
question.clue: Charles Guiteau proclaimed that he was a member of this faction after killing James Garfield.

swap.text: This Secretary of State under Grover Cleveland issued his "Corollary" during a border dispute between Britain and Venezuela.
swap.clue: This man served as Grover Cleveland's Attorney General and is best remembered for using judicial injunctions to help shut down the Pullman Strike.

question.leadin: The United States government has a sinister history of massacring Native Americans.
question.text: This incident took place on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in South Dakota. More than 150 men, women, and children from the Lakota Tribe were killed by James Forsyth's 7th Cavalry in this massacre.
question.clue: This event began after the deaf Black Coyote failed to respond to the order to give up his rifle, and was exacerbated by Yellow Bird's insistence that his shirt would deflect bullets.

swap.leadin: According to a story in the New York Times, this politician was caught seducing the Governor of Rhode Island's wife, after which the governor chased him out of his house with a musket.
swap.text: Name this 19th-century senator from New York. He led the Stalwart faction of the Republican Party against James G. Blaine's Half-Breeds.
swap.clue: To protest William H. Robertson's appointment as Port Collector, this man resigned from the Senate with his longtime ally Thomas C. Platt.

question.text: Its main hope was to persuade Congress to authorize a vast program of public works, financed by a substantial increase of money in circulation, and to provide jobs. It came to an ignominious end when its leader was arrested for trespassing on lawns at the Capitol. For 15 points - name this "army" which left Massillon, Ohio in March of 1894 and marched to Washington, D.C.
question.clue: The wife of its leader gave birth to a son named Legal Tender.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about some influential political cartoons in American history.
swap.text: An early color cartoon from Puck magazine lampooned this presidential candidate as the "tattooed man" whose body was covered in a sea of scandals. His namesake amendments barred government funding for parochial schools.
swap.clue: Samuel Burchard hurt this man's presidential bid after claiming that the other party represented "Rum, Romanism, and Rebellion".

question.leadin: In 1896, this future Georgian senator was seriously considered as a possible running mate for William Jennings Bryan on the Democratic platform.
question.text: As a representative, this man tried to require the Postal Service to deliver to rural areas for free, and he earned black support by condemning lynching, but was later prosecuted for his anti-Catholic newsletters.
question.clue: This editor of The Jefersonian covered the bejesus out of Frank's trial, because he wanted to use it to revive the Ku Klux Klan. This Georgia politician was the Populist Party nominee for President in both 1904 and 1908, afer which the party dis-banded.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about legends of the Wild West.
swap.text: The oft-romanticized 1881 gunfight between Wyatt Earp's posse and a group of villainous cowboys is usually named for this building in Tombstone, even though the fight actually took place in a lot adjacent to it.
swap.clue: The gunfight at this American location only was about 30 seconds and was between the Cochise County Cowboys and a group of officers that included Doc Holliday.

question.text: This man dubbed the conflict "a splendid little war" and helped negotiate the Paris treaty as Secretary of State under McKinley. He's also known for writing some ballads about Pike County.
question.clue: In a speech before Congress, this man claimed that American intervention in East Asia was unnecessary.

swap.leadin: This term was used by journalists to criticize gilded-age businessmen and their exploitative practices.
swap.text: Give this term that referred to ultra-wealthy industrialists such as John D. Rockefeller.
swap.clue: What derogatory two-word term was popularized in the Gilded Age to denote predatory business leaders who quashed competition, created monopolies, and paid subsistence wages?

question.text: A later Republican Congress doled out generous pensions for Civil War veterans and passed the Sherman Antitrust Act and the McKinley Tariff, leading opponents to give it this nickname.
question.clue: This U.S. Congress whose lavish spending earned it a derisive nickname.

swap.leadin: Under the pen name "Lonely Orphan Girl," this journalist wrote a letter to the editor in response to a column titled "What Girls Are Good For," earning her a job offer.
swap.text: Name this reporter who faked insanity to infiltrate the asylum on Blackwell Island, an experience that she detailed in Ten Days in a Mad House.
swap.clue: This person declared that "Mexico is a Republic in name only. It is the worst monarchy existence" in a nonfiction book based on her time living six months under the reign of Porfirio Diaz.

question.leadin: This man's namesake company offered a three million dollar loan to the state of Pennsylvania during the Civil War.
question.text: Identify this financier whose Northern Pacific Railway Company declared bankruptcy during the Panic of 1873.
question.clue: The "wire-house firm" concept was created by this man who financed the Northern Pacific Railway and tried to make Duluth a metropolis.

swap.leadin: This man served as Secretary of the Interior for Chester A. Arthur.
swap.text: Name this Republican Senator from Colorado, whose opposition to the gold standard caused him to found the splinter "Silver Republican" Party in 1896. He later became a Democrat.
swap.clue: This man led the Silver Republicans during the Election of 1896, most of whom supported Bryan. He also sponsored an amendment to an 1898 resolution that prevented the U.S. annexation of Cuba.

question.text: This 1894 tariff, which slightly reduced rates from the McKinley tariff of 1890, had as one of its provisions a graduated income tax struck down by the Supreme Court in 1895.
question.clue: The income tax provision that was struck down in Pollock had belonged to this piece of legislation.

swap.text: In 1869, Smith was a delegate at the founding convention of this political party, which according to many Republicans cost James G. Blaine the 1884 election by nominating spoiler candidate John St. John. This party won a statewide office exactly once, when Sidney Johnston Catts was elected governor of Florida in 1916.
swap.clue: They allowed Grover Cleveland to carry New York with the strong 1884 showing of John St. John, but their best results came in the next two presidential elections, in which Clinton Fisk and John Bidwell polled over 200,000 votes.
